en: The Theravāda Vinaya Mahāvibhaṅga:
The Section on Offenses Entailing Expiation (Pācittiyakaṇḍa)
The Chapter on False Speech, 2.
The Training Rule on Abusive Speech.
At that time, the Buddha, the Blessed One, was dwelling at Sāvatthī in Jeta’s Grove, Anāthapiṇḍika’s monastery.

Now at that time, the group-of-six monks, quarreling with well-behaved monks, insulted those well-behaved monks by birth, by name, by clan, by occupation, by craft, by illness, by physical marks, by defilement, and by offense; they reviled and ridiculed them even with low abuse.
Those monks who were of few desires... [and so on]... complained, grumbled, and became indignant.

“How indeed can the monks of the group of six, while quarreling with the well-behaved monks, revile those well-behaved monks—by means of their birth, their names, their clans, their occupations, their crafts, their illnesses, their physical marks, their defilements, or their offenses; and how can they insult and deride them even with base abuse?
Then those monks, having rebuked the monks of the group of six in many ways, reported this matter to the Blessed One... [as before]...
“Is it true, monks, that you, while quarreling with well-behaved monks, insulted those well-behaved monks—by [accusing them of] birth... and even by reviling and disparaging them with base abuse?
“It is true, Blessed One.
The Buddha, the Blessed One, rebuked them... [as before].
“How can you, foolish men, quarreling with well-behaved bhikkhus, insult those well-behaved bhikkhus—by [accusing them of] birth...
and by reviling and disparaging them even with base abuse?
This, foolish men, does not lead to the confidence of those without confidence... [and so on].”
Having rebuked him … and having given a discourse on the Dhamma, he addressed the monks:
“Once upon a time, monks, in Takkasilā there was a certain brahmin who had a bull named Nandivisāla.”
Then, monks, the ox Nandivisāla said this to that brahmin:
“Go, brahmin, together with the guild-president, perform a miracle for a thousand pieces of money:
‘My ox shall pull a hundred wagons loaded [to capacity].’”
Then, monks, that brahmin made a wager with the merchant for a thousand [coins]:
"My ox shall pull a hundred wagons loaded together.
Then, monks, having hitched up the hundred wagons and yoked the ox Nandivisāla, that brahmin said this:
“Go, Kūṭa! Pull, Kūṭa!
Then, monks, the ox Nandivisāla stood right there.
Thereupon, monks, that brahmin, defeated by a thousand [pieces of gold], fell into deep reflection.
Then, monks, the ox Nandivisāla said this to that brahmin:
“Brahmin, why are you brooding?
“Because, sir, I have been defeated by you for a thousand pieces,” he replied.
“But why, brahmin, do you seek to convict me, who am not guilty, with a false charge?
Go, brahmin, together with the merchant, perform a miracle with two thousand [pieces of gold]:
‘My ox shall pull a hundred wagons loaded [with goods].’”
‘Do not cause me to be guilty of a false accusation by speaking falsely.
Then, monks, that brahmin performed a miracle with the merchant for two thousand pieces [of gold], saying:
‘My ox shall pull a hundred wagons hitched together!’”
Then, monks, that brahmin, having hitched up a hundred carts and yoked the ox Nandivisāla, said this:
“Go, good one; pull, good one!
Then, monks, the ox Nandivisāla pulled away the hundred hitched-up carts.
One should speak only what is pleasing,
never what is displeasing;
for one who speaks what is pleasing, [the world will be favorable].
He cast off a heavy burden and obtained wealth;
because of that, he was delighted.
Even then, monks, I found censure and contempt unpleasant;
how much more so now would censure and contempt be pleasant?
This, monks, does not lead to the confidence of those without confidence... [and so on].
And thus, monks, you should recite this training rule:
"In the case of abusive speech, it is an offense of expiation (pācittiya).
Now, what is called "abusive speech"?
One reviles in ten ways: by birth, by name, by clan, by occupation, by craft, by illness, by physical marks, by defilement, by offense, and by abuse.
Regarding "birth," there are two kinds of birth: low birth and high birth.
Low birth means:
the caṇḍāla birth, the venaja birth, the nesāda birth, the rathakāra birth, the pukkusa birth. This is called low birth.
Noble birth means:
The khattiya caste and the brāhmaṇa caste—this is what is called a superior birth.
As for names, there are two kinds of names: the inferior name and the superior name.

An inferior name is one such as Avakaṇṇaka, Javakaṇṇaka, Dhaniṭṭhaka, Saviṭṭhaka, or Kulavaḍḍhaka; or whatever name in various regions is despised, looked down upon, reviled, disregarded, and treated with contempt—this is called an inferior name.
A superior name is one such as... [and so forth].

A name connected with the Buddha, connected with the Dhamma, connected with the Saṅgha, or one that is not despised, not disparaged, not ridiculed, not held in contempt, but rather esteemed in various regions—that is called a "superior" name.
As for "clan," there are two types of clans: lowly clans and superior clans.

A low clan is that which is the Kosiya clan or the Bhāradvāja clan, or whatever clans in various regions are despised, held in contempt, reviled, disregarded, and treated with disrespect; this is called a low clan.
A high clan is as follows:

The Gotama clan, the Moggallāna clan, the Kaccāna clan, the Vāsiṭṭha clan, or whatever clans are not unknown, not despised, not reviled, nor held in contempt in various regions, but are esteemed—this is called a superior clan.
As for action, there are two kinds of action: inferior action and superior action.
Inferior work is called:

the work of a watchman, the work of a flower-scavenger, or whatever work in various regions is despised, looked down upon, scorned, treated with contempt, and disregarded; this is called inferior work.
Noble work is called: [the rest].

Agriculture, trade, and cattle-rearing—or whatever in various regions is not despised, not looked down upon, not scorned, not treated with contempt, but is held in high esteem. This is called "excellent" work (*ukkaṭṭha-kamma*).
As for "craft" (*sippa*), there are two kinds of crafts: inferior craft and excellent craft.
An inferior craft is that of a reed-worker, a potter, a weaver, a leather-worker, or a barber;
or whatever craft in various regions is despised, looked down upon, reviled, disregarded, and held in low esteem. This is what is called an inferior craft.
A "superior craft" (ukkaṭṭhaṃ sippaṃ) means:

finger-calculation, arithmetic, and writing; or whatever in various regions is not despised, not looked down upon, not reviled, not treated with contempt, but is held in high esteem—that is called a superior craft.
All diseases, moreover, are inferior.
Moreover, the affliction of diabetes mellitus is severe.
As for "sign," there are two kinds of signs: the inferior sign and the superior sign.
An inferior mark is one that is too long, too short, too dark, or too pale; this is called an inferior mark.
A superior mark is as follows:
Neither too tall, nor too short, neither too dark, nor too fair—this is called the superior characteristic.
All defilements are inferior;
all offenses are inferior.
Moreover, the attainment of stream-entry is the highest.
As for "abuse," there are two kinds of abuse: low abuse and high abuse.
A "low" insult is as follows: "You are a camel!
You are a ram! You are an ox! You are a donkey! You are an animal! You are destined for hell! There is no happy rebirth for you;
only an unhappy rebirth is to be expected for you! Or [insults using] the syllable *ya* or the syllable *bha*, or [insults involving] a *kāṭakoṭacikā* (a type of thorny plant).
Or, this is called an inferior insult.
A superior insult is as follows:

"You are wise, you are competent, you are intelligent, you are learned, you are an expounder of the Dhamma; there is no miserable rebirth for you; you may expect only a happy destination"—this is called a superior insult.

If one who is ordained, desiring to revile, despise, or humiliate another who is ordained, speaks of a low person as being low—saying of a caṇḍāla, a vena, a nesāda, a rathakāra, or a pukkusas, “You are a caṇḍāla! You are a vena! You are a nesāda! You are a rathakāra!
You are a pukkusas!”—there is an offense for every word; for each word, it is a *pācittiya*.
If one who is ordained, desiring to revile, despise, or humiliate another who is ordained,
speaks of a superior person in terms of inferiority— saying to a Kṣatriya or a Brāhmaṇa, "You are a Caṇḍāla, you are a Veṇa, you are a Nesāda, you are a Rathakāra, you are a Pukkusa"—
there is an offense for each word; for each word, it is a *pācittiya*.

If one who is ordained, desiring to revile, despise, or humiliate another who is ordained, speaks of a superior person as inferior—saying of a Caṇḍāla, a Vena, a Nesāda, a Rathakāra, or a Pukkusa, "You are a Khattiya!
You are a Brāhmaṇa!"—there is an offense for every word; for each word, it is a *pācittiya*.
If one who is ordained, desiring to revile, despise, or humiliate another who is ordained,

speaks of a superior person as superior— saying to a khattiya or a brāhmaṇa, "You are a khattiya, you are a brāhmaṇa"— there is an offense for each word, a *pācittiya* for each word. If one who is ordained,

desiring to revile, despise, or humiliate another who is ordained, speaks of an inferior person as inferior— saying [of them] "Avakaṇṇaka," "Javakaṇṇaka," "Dhaniṭṭhaka," "Saviṭṭhaka," or "Kulavaḍḍhaka"— [there is an offense].
If one says, “You are earless,” “You are quick-eared,” “You are Dhaniṭṭha,” “You are Saviṭṭha,” or “You are a family-increaser,” there is an offense entailing confession for every such utterance.
If one who is fully ordained, desiring to revile, to disparage, or to humiliate another who is fully ordained, speaks of a superior person by means of an inferior term—
such as addressing Buddharakkhita, Dhammarakkhita, or Saṅgharakkhita as “earless,” “quick-eared,” [and so forth]— [there is an offense].
“You are a Dhaniṭṭhaka,” “You are a Saviṭṭhaka,” “You are a Kulavaḍḍhaka”— if he says this, there is an offense of expiation for each statement.
If one who is fully ordained, desiring to revile, deride, or humiliate another who is fully ordained, speaks of a superior person in terms of an inferior one—
calling them a “Down-eared,” a “Quick-eared,” a “Dhaniṭṭhaka,” a “Saviṭṭhaka,” or a “Kulavaḍḍhaka”— or saying, “You are a Buddharakkhita,” [there is an offense].
If one says, "You are protected by the Dhamma; you are protected by the Saṅgha," there is an offense of wrong speech, an offense of *pācittiya* for each utterance.

If one who is fully ordained, desiring to revile, despise, or humiliate another who is fully ordained, speaks of a superior person in terms of superiority—referring to one protected by the Buddha, one protected by the Dhamma, or one protected by the Saṅgha—saying, "You are protected by the Buddha; you are protected by the Dhamma... [and so forth].
If he says, “You are Saṅgharakkhita,” there is an offense of expiation for each word spoken.

If one who is fully ordained, desiring to revile, despise, or humiliate another who is fully ordained, speaks of the low by means of the low, saying of a Kosiya Bhāradvāja, “You are a Kosiya, you are a Bhāradvāja,” there is an offense of expiation for each word spoken.
If one who is fully ordained, desiring to revile, despise, or humiliate another who is fully ordained, speaks of the high by means of the low...
If one says, "He calls Gotama, Moggallāna, Kaccāna, or Vāsiṭṭha," or says, "Are you a Kosian?
Are you a Bhāradvāja?", there is an offense of wrong speech; by each word, there is an offense of expiation (pācittiya).
If one who is fully ordained, desiring to revile, despise, or humiliate another who is fully ordained, [addresses them] with something superior as something inferior...
If one says, "Kosiya," to Bhāradvāja, or says, "Are you Gotama? Are you Moggallāna? Are you Kaccāna? Are you Vāsiṭṭha?
there is an offense of wrong speech; by each word, there is an offense entailing expiation (pācittiya).
If one who is fully ordained, desiring to revile, to disparage, or to humiliate another who is fully ordained, [addresses them] with a superior [name] to a superior [name]...
If one says, "You are Gotama, Moggallāna, Kaccāna, or Vāsiṭṭha," addressing a person who has received full ordination as "Gotama! You are Moggallāna! You are Kaccāna!
You are Vāsiṭṭha!"—there is an offense of expiation for each word spoken.

If one who has received full ordination, desiring to revile, to disparage, or to humiliate another who has received full ordination, speaks of them in a low manner using a low term... [there is an offense].
If one says to a watchman who discards flowers, "You are a watchman! You are a flower-discarder!", there is an offense for every word;
it is an *pācittiya* for each word.

If one who is fully ordained, desiring to revile, despise, or humiliate another who is fully ordained, speaks of a superior person by means of an inferior one—such as a farmer, a merchant, or a cowherd—[there is an offense].
If he says, "You are a watchman! You are a flower-scavenger!", there is an offense for each word, a *pācittiya* for each word.

If one who is fully ordained, desiring to revile, despise, or humiliate another who is fully ordained, speaks of the superior as inferior—saying of a watchman or a flower-scavenger, "You are a farmer! You are a merchant! You are a cattle-herder!"—there is an offense.
By speech, by speech, it is an offense of expiation (*pācittiya*).
If one who is fully ordained, desiring to revile, desiring to disparage, or desiring to humiliate another who is fully ordained, speaks of a superior person in superior terms—
such as a farmer, a merchant, or a cattle-herder— and says, "You are a farmer," "You are a merchant," or "You are a cattle-herder," [it is an offense].
There is an offense by speech; by speech, it is an offense of expiation (pācittiya).

If one who is fully ordained, desiring to revile, desiring to disparage, or desiring to humiliate another who is fully ordained, speaks of a lowly person as lowly—such as a reed-worker, a potter, a weaver, a leather-worker, or a barber—saying, "You are a reed-worker! You are a potter!"... [and so forth].
If one says, "You are a weaver, you are a leather-worker, you are a barber," there is an offense of wrong speech; for every such utterance, there is an offense of expiation (pācittiya).

If one who is fully ordained, desiring to revile, despise, or humiliate another who is fully ordained, speaks of a superior person in terms of an inferior trade—such as a finger-counter, an accountant, a scribe, a basket-maker, a potter, a weaver, or a leather-worker—[there is an offense].
If he says, "You are a barber," there is an offense of wrong speech; by that speech, it is an offense of expiation (pācittiya).

If one who is fully ordained, desiring to revile, despise, or humiliate another who is fully ordained, speaks of a superior person in terms of an inferior one—such as a reed-worker, a potter, a weaver, a leather-worker, or a barber—saying, "You are a calculator, you are an accountant..."

If one who is fully ordained, desiring to revile, deride, or humiliate another who is fully ordained, speaks of the superior in terms of the superior—saying to a finger-calculator, an accountant, or a scribe: "You are a finger-calculator! You are an accountant! You are a scribe!"—there is an offense; for every word, there is an offense of expiation (pācittiya). If one who is fully ordained... [repeats the same structure]. There is an offense.
By speech, by speech, it is an offense of expiation (pācittiya).

If one who is fully ordained, desiring to revile, desiring to mock, or desiring to humiliate another who is fully ordained, speaks of a low thing with a low thing—[saying of one who has] leprosy, a boil, ringworm, consumption, or epilepsy: "You have leprosy! You have a boil! You have ringworm!"—[it is an offense].
If one says, "You are a leper; you are a tumor-patient; you are a skin-disease patient; you are a consumptive; you are an epileptic," there is an offense of expiation for each statement.
If one who is ordained, desiring to revile, disparage, or humiliate another who is ordained, speaks of a superior person with inferior terms—such as addressing a diabetic as:
"You are a leper; you are a tumor-patient; you are a skin-disease patient; you are a consumptive; you are an epileptic"—[there is an offense].
If he speaks, there is an offense by speech; [he incurs] a *pācittiya* offense by speech.

Should one who is fully ordained, desiring to revile, desiring to deride, or desiring to humiliate another who is fully ordained, speak of a superior person as inferior—saying of one afflicted with leprosy (*kuṭṭhika*), boils (*gaṇḍika*), scabs (*kilāsika*), consumption (*sosika*), or epilepsy (*apamārika*)—“You are a diabetic (*madhumehika*)”; [he incurs an offense].
There is an offense by speech; by each word, there is an offense of expiation (*pācittiya*).

If one who is fully ordained, desiring to revile, deride, or humiliate another who is fully ordained, speaks of the superior with the superior—that is, if he says to one suffering from diabetes, "You are a diabetic"—there is an offense by speech; by each word, there is an offense of expiation.
If one who is fully ordained, desiring to revile, deride, or humiliate another who is fully ordained, speaks of the inferior with the inferior...

If one says of someone who is too tall, too short, too dark, or too fair, "You are too tall," "You are too short," "You are too dark," or "You are too fair," there is an offense of expiation for each such utterance.
If one who is fully ordained, desiring to revile, to deride, or to humiliate another who is fully ordained, [uses] the inferior to disparage the superior...

If he says, "Speak," or if he speaks what is neither too long, nor too short, nor too dark, nor too bright— saying, "You are too tall," "You are too short," "You are too dark," or "You are too bright"—
there is an offense for each word, a *pācittiya* for each word. If one who is fully ordained,
desiring to revile, to mock, or to humiliate another who is fully ordained, [speaks] the superior as inferior...
If one says, "You are too tall, too short, too dark, or too fair," and says, "You are not too tall, you are not too short, you are not too dark,
you are not too fair," there is an offense of expiation for each statement.
If one who is ordained, desiring to revile, to mock, or to humiliate another who is ordained, [speaks] the superior with reference to the superior...

If one says, "Not too tall, not too short, not too dark, not too fair"— saying, "You are not too tall, you are not too short, you are not too dark, you are not too fair"— there is an offense of wrong speech,

an offense of *pācittiya* for each word. If one who is fully ordained, desiring to revile, despise, or humiliate another who is fully ordained, speaks of the inferior as inferior, there is an offense of wrong speech, an offense of *pācittiya* for each word.
If one who is obsessed by lust, obsessed by hatred, or obsessed by delusion says, "You are obsessed by lust, you are obsessed by hatred,
you are obsessed by delusion," there is an offense of expiation for each word spoken.
If one who is fully ordained, desiring to revile, desiring to disparage, or desiring to humiliate another who is fully ordained, [accuses them] of something low while they are superior...
If one says to someone who is free from lust, free from hatred, and free from delusion, "You are obsessed by lust; you are obsessed by hatred;
you are obsessed by delusion," there is an offense of wrong speech, an offense of *pācittiya* for each word spoken.
If one who is fully ordained, desiring to revile, to mock, or to humiliate another who is fully ordained, [speaks] of the superior as inferior...

If one says to someone who is obsessed by lust, obsessed by hatred, or obsessed by delusion, "You are free from lust, you are free from hatred, you are free from delusion," there is an offense of wrong speech;
it is an offense of expiation (pācittiya) for each word.
If one who is fully ordained, desiring to revile, to despise, or to humiliate another who is fully ordained, [addresses them] with the superior [title] to the superior...
If one says of someone who is free from lust, free from hatred, and free from delusion, "You are free from lust, you are free from hatred, you are free from delusion," there is an offense by speech,
an offense of expiation (pācittiya) for that speech.
If one who is fully ordained, desiring to revile, to disparage, or to humiliate another who is fully ordained, speaks of the low as being low, [there is an offense].

one who has committed an offense entailing expulsion, one who has committed an offense entailing suspension from the Saṅgha, one who has committed a grave offense, one who has committed an offense entailing confession, one who has committed an offense entailing acknowledgment, one who has committed an offense of wrong-doing, or one who has committed an offense of wrong speech—"You have committed an offense entailing expulsion;
you have committed an offense entailing suspension from the Saṅgha; you have committed a grave offense; you have committed an offense entailing confession..."

If one says, "You have committed an offense," "You have committed an offense entailing confession (pāṭidesanīya)," "You have committed an offense of wrong-doing (dukkaṭa)," or "You have committed an offense of improper speech (dubbhāsita)," there is an offense for every word, namely, a pācittiya for every word.
If one who is fully ordained, desiring to revile, deride, or humiliate another who is fully ordained, [accuses them] with something inferior [of something] superior...
If he says to one who is a stream-enterer, "You have committed an offense entailing expulsion" ...
[or] "You have committed an offense of wrong speech," there is an offense for each word, an offense of expiation for each word.
If one who is fully ordained, desiring to revile, to mock, or to humiliate another who is fully ordained, [speaks] of the superior as inferior...
If one says to someone who has committed a *pārājika* offense... [or] to someone who has committed an *dubbhāsita* offense, "You are a stream-enterer," there is an offense for each word;
for each word, it is a *pācittiya*.

If one who is fully ordained, desiring to revile, to disparage, or to humiliate another who is fully ordained, speaks of a superior person in terms of a superior quality, saying to a stream-enterer, "You are a stream-enterer," there is an offense for each word; for each word, it is a *pācittiya*.
One who is ordained, desiring to revile, despise, or humiliate another who is ordained, speaks of one who is low as being low:
"You are a camel, you are a ram, you are an ox, you are a donkey, you are an animal, you are a denizen of hell!
You are not destined for a good rebirth; for you there is only an evil destiny."
...is to be expected,” he says, there is an offense of wrong speech; for every word, there is an offense entailing expiation (pācittiya).

If one who is fully ordained, desiring to revile, deride, or humiliate another who is fully ordained, speaks of a superior person with inferior terms—[describing] one who is wise, competent, intelligent, learned, and an expositor of the Dhamma—as: “You are a camel! You are a ram! You are an ox!”...
"You are a donkey; you are an animal; you are a denizen of hell; there is no good destination for you;
only a bad destination is to be expected for you"—if he speaks thus, it is an offense of expiation (pācittiya) for each word.
If one who is fully ordained, desiring to revile, to mock, or to humiliate another who is fully ordained, [speaks] the superior as inferior...
If he says to a goat, a ram, a bull, a donkey, an animal, or a denizen of hell:
"You are wise, you are competent, you are intelligent, you are learned, you are an expounder of the Dhamma; there is no miserable destination for you;
only a happy destination is to be expected for you," there is an offense for each word, a *pācittiya* for each word.

A person who has received full ordination, wishing to revile, disparage, or humiliate another who has received full ordination, speaks of one who is superior as being superior—a wise man, one who is competent, intelligent, learned, and a preacher of the Dhamma—saying: "You are wise; you are competent;
you are intelligent; you are learned; you are a preacher of the Dhamma; there is no bad destination for you; for you there is only a good destination."
If one says, “It is to be expected,” there is an offense by speech: an offense of expiation (pācittiya) for each word.

If one who is ordained, desiring to revile, despise, or humiliate another who is ordained, speaks thus: “There are here some outcasts, bamboo-workers, hunters, chariot-makers, and scavengers,” there is an offense by speech: an offense of wrong-doing (dukkaṭa) for each word.

If one who is ordained, desiring to revile, despise, or humiliate another who is ordained, speaks thus: “There are here some kṣatriyas and brahmins,” there is an offense by speech: an offense of wrong-doing for each word.
If one who is ordained, desiring to revile, despise, or humiliate another who is ordained, speaks thus: “There are some here who are earless, half-eared, with drooping ears, with thick ears,
or who increase the family,” he says this… [and so on]… “There are some here who are protected by the Buddha, protected by the Dhamma,
or protected by the Saṅgha,” he says this… [and so on]… “There are some here who are Kosiya-clansmen or Bhāradvāja-clansmen,” he says this… [and so on].

“There are some here who are Gotamas, Moggallānas, Kaccānas, or Vāsiṭṭhas,” he says … [and so on] … “There are some here who are builders or flower-scavengers,” he says … [and so on] … “There are some here who are farmers,
merchants, or cattle-herders,” he says … [and so on].
“Here there are some reed-workers, potters, weavers, leather-workers, and barbers,” he says… [and so on]… “Here there are some finger-calculators,
accountants, and scribes,” he says… [and so on]… “Here there are some afflicted with leprosy,
boils, ringworm, consumption, and epilepsy,” he says… [and so on].
“Here there are some who suffer from diabetes,” he says… [and so on]… “Here there are some who are too tall, too short, too dark,
or too fair,” he says… [and so on]… “Here there are some who are neither too tall nor too short, neither too dark nor too fair,” he says… [and so on].
“There are some here who are obsessed by lust, obsessed by hatred, and obsessed by delusion,” he says... [and so on]...
“There are some here who are free from lust, free from hatred, and free from delusion,” he says... [and so on]...
“There are some here who have committed an offense entailing expulsion (pārājika)... [and so on]...”
...saying, "They have committed an offense of wrong speech" ...pe...
saying, "There are some here who are stream-enterers" ...pe...

saying, "There are some here—camels, rams, oxen, donkeys, animals, or those bound for hell; there is no good destination for them, only an evil destination is to be expected for them," there is an offense of wrong-doing for each word spoken.
If one who is ordained, desiring to revile, despise, or humiliate another who is ordained, speaks thus:
"There are here certain wise, competent, intelligent, learned, and preachers of the Dhamma; for them there is no miserable destination;
only a happy destination is to be expected for them," he commits an offense for each statement, an offense of wrong-doing (dukkaṭa) for every word spoken.

If one who is ordained, desiring to revile, despise, or humiliate another who is ordained, speaks thus: “Surely they are outcasts, bamboo-workers, hunters, cartwrights, or scavengers,” there is an offense for each word, an offense of wrong-doing (dukkaṭa) for each word.

…pe… If one who is ordained, desiring to revile, despise, or humiliate another who is ordained, speaks thus: “Surely they are wise, competent, intelligent, learned, and preachers of the Dhamma,” there is an offense for each word, an offense of wrong-doing for each word.
If one who is ordained, desiring to revile, despise, or humiliate another who is ordained, says: “We are not Caṇḍālas, Veṇas, Nesādas, Rathakāras, or Pukkusas,” he speaks thus...

[and so on]... “We are not wise, competent, intelligent, learned, or speakers on the Dhamma; there is no bad destination for us; we can only expect a good destination. For every word, there is an offense of wrong-doing (dukkaṭa).
If one who is ordained, desiring to revile, despise, or humiliate one who is unordained, speaks of the low as low... [and so on]...
One speaks of the superior as inferior; ... [and so on] ...
one speaks of the inferior as superior; ...
[and so on] ... one speaks of the superior as superior—a person who is wise, competent, intelligent, learned, and a preacher of the Dhamma.
If one says, “You are wise, you are competent, you are intelligent, you are learned, you are an expounder of the Dhamma; there is no bad destination for you;
only a good destination is to be expected for you,” there is an offense of wrong-doing for each word spoken.

If one who is fully ordained, desiring to revile, despise, or humiliate one who is not fully ordained, speaks thus: “There are here some Caṇḍālas, Veṇas, Nesādas, Rathakāras, and Pukkusas,” he speaks… [and so on].

“If there are here some who are wise, competent, intelligent, learned, and speakers on the Dhamma, for them there is no bad destination; a good destination is to be expected for them,” he says—there is an offense for each word, an offense of wrong-doing (dukkaṭa) for each word.

If one who is fully ordained, desiring to revile, despise, or humiliate one who is not fully ordained, speaks thus: “Surely those who are Caṇḍālas, Veṇas, Nesādas, Rathakāras, and Pukkusas”—he says [this] … [and so on].
If he says, “Surely these are wise, competent, intelligent, learned, and preachers of the Dhamma,” there is an offense of wrong-doing for each word.

If one who is fully ordained, desiring to revile, despise, or humiliate one who is not fully ordained, speaks thus: “We are not outcasts, bamboo-workers, hunters, chariot-makers, or scavengers,” there is an offense of wrong-doing for each word. …pe… (and so on).

“We are not wise, nor proficient, nor intelligent, nor learned, nor preachers of the Dhamma; there is no bad destination for us; we expect only a good destination,” he says. There is an offense of wrong-doing (dukkaṭa) for every word spoken.

If one who is fully ordained, not wishing to revile, not wishing to insult, nor wishing to humiliate another who is fully ordained, speaks of a low person as low out of a desire for sport—saying of a caṇḍāla, a vena, a nesāda, a rathakāra, or a pukkusa: “You are a caṇḍāla! You are a vena!”—[there is an offense].
If one says, "You are a hunter, you are a chariot-maker, you are a scavenger," there is an offense of wrong speech for each word spoken.
If one who is ordained, not wishing to revile, not wishing to disparage, and not wishing to humiliate another who is ordained,

speaks of a superior person in terms of an inferior one out of a desire for sport— such as saying of a Kṣatriya or a Brāhmaṇa, "You are a Caṇḍāla, you are a Veṇa, you are a Nesāda, you are a Rathakāra"— [there is an offense].
If one says, "Are you a Pukkusa?", there is an offense of wrong speech for each word spoken.
If one who is fully ordained does not intend to revile, nor to disparage, nor to humiliate another who is fully ordained,
but speaks of a superior person as inferior out of a desire for sport— saying of a Caṇḍāla, a Vena, a Nesāda, a Rathakāra, or a Pukkusa, "You are a Kṣatriya"— [there is an offense].
If he says, "You are a brahmin," there is an offense of wrong speech for each word spoken.
If one who is ordained, not wishing to revile, not wishing to disparage, and not wishing to humiliate another who is ordained,
but desiring sport, speaks of the superior as superior— saying to a khattiya or a brahmin, "You are a khattiya" or "You are a brahmin"— [there is an offense].
There is an offense for speech; there is an offense of wrong speech.

One who is fully ordained, not wishing to revile, not wishing to disparage, and not wishing to humiliate another who is fully ordained, speaks base things about the base out of a desire for sport … [and so on] … speaks superior things about the base … [and so on].

If one speaks of the inferior by means of the superior …pe… or if one speaks of the superior by means of the superior—that is, regarding one who is wise, competent, intelligent, learned, and a preacher of the Dhamma—if one says:

"You are wise, you are competent, you are intelligent, you are learned, you are a preacher of the Dhamma; there is no bad destination for you; only a good destination is to be expected for you," there is an offense for every word spoken, an offense of wrong speech.

If one who is ordained, not wishing to revile, not wishing to disparage, and not wishing to humiliate another who is ordained, speaks thus out of a desire for fun: "There are here some caṇḍālas, veṇas, nesādas, rathakāras, and pukkusas," he speaks... [and so on] ...

"There are here some wise, competent, intelligent, learned, and preachers of the Dhamma; there is no bad destination for them; a good destination alone is to be expected for them. For every word, he commits an offense of wrong speech.
One who is ordained, not wishing to revile, nor wishing to disparage, nor wishing to humiliate another who is ordained, but speaking out of a desire for sport, says:

“Surely these are Caṇḍālas, Veṇas, Nesādas, Rathakāras, or Pukkusas,” he speaks thus… [and so on]… “Surely these are wise, competent, intelligent, learned, and preachers of the Dhamma,” he speaks thus; there is an offense of wrong speech for each word spoken.

If one who is ordained, not wishing to revile, not wishing to disparage, and not wishing to humiliate another who is ordained, speaks thus out of a desire for sport: “We are not Caṇḍālas, we are not Veṇas, we are not Nesādas, we are not Rathakāras, we are not Pukkusas,” he speaks... [and so on] ...

“We are not wise, we are not competent, we are not intelligent, we are not learned, we are not preachers of the Dhamma; there is no bad destination for us; only a good destination is to be expected for us. For every word, there is an offense of wrong speech.
One who is fully ordained, not wishing to revile, not wishing to disparage, and not wishing to humiliate one who is not fully ordained, out of a desire for sport,
speaks of the low as low … [and so on] … speaks of the low as high … [and so on] … speaks of the high as low … [and so on].

If one praises the superior with the superior—that is, a wise, competent, intelligent, learned person who is a preacher of the Dhamma—by saying, "You are wise, you are competent, you are intelligent, you are learned, you are a preacher of the Dhamma;
there is no bad destination for you; only a good destination is to be expected for you," there is an offense for each word spoken, an offense of wrong speech.

One who is ordained, not wishing to revile, nor wishing to disparage, nor wishing to humiliate one who is unordained, speaks thus out of a desire for mere sport: “There are here some Caṇḍālas, Veṇas, Nesādas, Rathakāras, and Pukkusas,” he says... [and so on]...

“There are here some wise, competent, intelligent, learned, and preachers of the Dhamma; there is no bad destination for them; only a good destination is to be expected for them. He says this: for every word, there is an offense of wrong speech.

One who is ordained, not wishing to revile, not wishing to disparage, and not wishing to humiliate one who is unordained, speaks thus out of a desire for sport: "Who indeed are these outcasts, bamboo-workers, hunters, chariot-makers, and scavengers?"—if he says this...
[and so on] ...or if he says, "Who indeed are these wise, competent, intelligent, learned, and preachers of the Dhamma?"—there is an offense for each word, an offense of wrong speech.

One who is fully ordained, not wishing to revile, not wishing to disparage, and not wishing to humiliate one who is not fully ordained, says this out of a desire for sport: “We are not Caṇḍālas, we are not Veṇas, we are not Nesādas, we are not Rathakāras, we are not Pukkusas,” he says...

[and so on]... “We are not wise, we are not competent, we are not intelligent, we are not learned, we are not preachers of the Dhamma; there is no bad destination for us; only a good destination is to be expected for us. For each such statement, there is an offense of wrong speech. There is no offense—
one who has the welfare as the primary concern,
one who has the Dhamma as the primary concern,
and one who has the instruction as the primary concern.
For one who is insane,
for one whose mind is deranged,
for one overwhelmed by pain.
"For one who is a first-time offender.
The second training rule on slanderous speech is concluded.
